snippets: To guarantee true idempotency under concurrency, systems must enforce atomic database-level constraints, configure explicit transaction isolation levels (or immediate exclusive locks), and implement jittered exponential backoff retries against lock contention. The implementation pattern outlined below relies on a three-tier defense model: flowchart TD subgraph ClientLayer ["Client Layer"] Req["Concurrent Inbound Webhooks"] end subgraph DefensePipeline ["Deduplication Pipeline"] Lock["1.

Treat database-level unique constraints as your non-negotiable final line of defense. Pair lock recovery with truncated exponential backoff to absorb burst contention gracefully. By treating concurrency control and transaction isolation as primary architectural concerns, webhook ingestion pipelines remain resilient, deterministic, and fully idempotent under high-scale production load.

Under sustained concurrency, explicit serialization increases lock contention (OperationalError: database is locked). Rejecting requests immediately degrades availability. Instead, pairing short retry loops with millisecond-scale exponential backoff resolves transient contention while maintaining high system throughput. The following verification harness simulates 20 concurrent inbound webhook deliveries hitting a shared in-memory database within the same millisecond window.

In event-driven architectures, deduplicating asynchronous webhooks is frequently handled with a naive application-level pattern: check if the incoming event_id exists in the database, and skip processing if a record is found. When implemented as an uncoordinated SELECT followed by an INSERT, this pattern introduces a classic Check-Then-Act race condition (TOCTOU: Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use) that breaks down under concurrent traffic:

Atomic Lock Acquisition: Utilizing Redis's atomic SET key value NX EX  command guarantees that checking for key existence and acquiring the lease occurs as a single atomic CPU instruction within Redis, preventing thread and process race conditions without requiring heavy distributed consensus protocols. Breaking the Retry Loop: If an incoming webhook fails to acquire the lock (indicating an identical request is currently in-flight or was previously processed), the application server must immediately return a 200 OK status. Returning 4xx or 5xx causes third-party delivery engines to perceive a delivery failure, amplifying traffic into a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) retry storm.

Lack of Multi-Process Shared State: An in-memory dictionary (self._store) is scoped strictly to the memory space of a single OS process. web.title: Transaction | SQLite Cloud Docs
web.description: Any command that accesses the database will automatically start a transaction if one is not already in effect.
snippets: If a writer cannot obtain the lock, it uses SQLite’s busy-handler to pause and retry for a while: ... If there is significant contention for the writer lock, this mechanism can be inefficient. In this case it is better for the application to use a mutex or some other mechanism that supports blocking to ensure that at most one writer is attempting to COMMIT a BEGIN CONCURRENT transaction at a time.

Usually, SQLite allows at most one writer to proceed concurrently. The BEGIN CONCURRENT enhancement allows multiple writers to process write transactions simultanously if the database is in “wal” or “wal2” mode, although the system still serializes COMMIT commands. When a write-transaction is opened with “BEGIN CONCURRENT”, actually locking the database is deferred until a COMMIT is executed.

If all database clients (readers and writers) are located in the same OS process, and if that OS is a Unix variant, then it can be more efficient to the built-in VFS “unix-excl” instead of the default “unix”. This is because it uses more efficient locking primitives. The key to maximizing concurrency using BEGIN CONCURRENT is to ensure that there are a large number of non-conflicting transactions. In SQLite, each table and each index is stored as a separate b-tree, each of which is distributed over a discrete set of database pages.

This means that any number of transactions started with BEGIN CONCURRENT may proceed concurrently. The system uses optimistic page-level-locking to prevent conflicting concurrent transactions from being committed.
